subsystems.name: Individual nanobot
subsystems.role: the basic unit: a molecule-scale machine that senses, moves and acts.
parts: chassis (e.g. DNA origami or protein cage)

subsystems.name: Swarm coordination layer
subsystems.role: lets billions of units act together without a central controller.

subsystems.name: Power and propulsion
subsystems.role: supplies energy for movement and computation inside the body.

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and assembly
subsystems.role: produces identical units in enormous numbers.

subsystems.name: Navigation and targeting
subsystems.role: guides the swarm to a specific tissue or material defect.

subsystems.name: Payload and safety
subsystems.role: performs the task and can be shut down or cleared from the body.

buildSteps.title: Design the unit
buildSteps.detail: Choose a molecular chassis and integrate sensing, actuation and communication elements into a single nanoscale machine.

buildSteps.title: Synthesize components
buildSteps.detail: Produce the building blocks using chemical synthesis, recombinant DNA or protein engineering.

buildSteps.title: Self-assemble nanobots
buildSteps.detail: Use molecular self-assembly to combine components into functional units, often in solution.

buildSteps.title: Scale production
buildSteps.detail: Adapt biological or microfluidic methods to manufacture billions of identical units with high yield.

buildSteps.title: Program swarm behaviour
buildSteps.detail: Encode local rules for stigmergic communication so simple interactions produce coordinated group tasks.

buildSteps.title: Test in vitro
buildSteps.detail: Observe small swarms in microfluidic chips, measuring movement, communication and task completion.

buildSteps.title: Animal trials
buildSteps.detail: Introduce swarms into animal models to test biocompatibility, targeting and clearance.

buildSteps.title: Clinical and field use
buildSteps.detail: After human trials and safety approval, deploy with external imaging and reliable shutdown controls.

prerequisites.why: simple structures are routine, but functional robots with integrated parts are not yet demonstrated.
no compact, long-lasting power source exists at this scale for operation inside the body.
algorithms exist for macro robots, but chemical communication between molecules is hard to control.
deep-tissue tracking of individual nanobots is not yet possible.
making billions of identical, functional units is far beyond current production methods.
degradable materials exist, but reliable off-switches for swarms are not demonstrated.

pathway.milestone: individual molecular machines and simple micro/nanorobots demonstrated in lab
pathway.unlocks: basic components and proof of concept.

pathway.milestone: small swarms (thousands) in vitro performing simple tasks like targeted release
in vivo animal trials for localized therapy, with external guidance
human trials for specific conditions, then autonomous repair in materials
pathway.unlocks: routine medical and industrial use, if safety is proven.
